name: David
charge: A man after the Lord's own heart; keeping his commandments and following him with all his heart, save only in the matter of Uriah
summary: Shepherd, giant-killer, hunted man who twice had Saul in his hand and would not touch the Lord's anointed, king who danced before the ark and would not build a house until told he could. The Lord made a covenant with his house that has a Son sitting on it for ever. His one great fall is its own case; this is the rest.
offense: David was taken from keeping sheep to feed Israel. Samuel first looked upon Jesse's older son, but the Lord corrected the measure: man looks upon appearance; the Lord looks upon the heart (1 Samuel 16:6-13). Psalms 78:70-72 joins David's shepherding of the flock to the integrity and skill with which he fed the nation. The calling required the same care on a greater charge. Before he held the throne, he served the king who would come to hate him. He played for Saul's relief, went where Saul sent him, and behaved wisely while Saul's envy grew (1 Samuel 16:21-23; 18:5-16). Twice Saul was placed within his reach, and twice David refused to kill him. Even cutting the skirt of Saul's robe troubled his heart (1 Samuel 24:4-7; 26:8-12). He would not use a promised kingdom to justify taking the life of the Lord's anointed.
judgment: Thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever. Therefore the Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight. The sure mercies of David. He gave them a king, David, to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will. Of this man's seed hath God according to his promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus.
offenseFull: David was taken from keeping sheep to feed Israel. Samuel first looked upon Jesse's older son, but the Lord corrected the measure: man looks upon appearance; the Lord looks upon the heart (1 Samuel 16:6-13). Psalms 78:70-72 joins David's shepherding of the flock to the integrity and skill with which he fed the nation. The calling required the same care on a greater charge.

Before he held the throne, he served the king who would come to hate him. He played for Saul's relief, went where Saul sent him, and behaved wisely while Saul's envy grew (1 Samuel 16:21-23; 18:5-16). Twice Saul was placed within his reach, and twice David refused to kill him. Even cutting the skirt of Saul's robe troubled his heart (1 Samuel 24:4-7; 26:8-12). He would not use a promised kingdom to justify taking the life of the Lord's anointed.

entries.commentary: Chapter 13 is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the beginning of the proof that he is not fit to be king over Israel. Saul chose three thousand men, two thousand with him in Michmash and mount Bethel and a thousand with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it; Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, and Israel was had in abomination with the Philistines. His son popped off the battle, so now it is war time.

The Philistines gathered thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand on the seashore, far deeper than the three thousand Israel had prepared. When the men of Israel saw they were in a strait, they hid themselves in caves, thickets, rocks, high places, and pits; some Hebrews fled over Jordan, and the people that followed Saul followed him trembling. The sons of God, the mighty men of valor, saw the enemy coming and started hiding. As the chosen people, if we really have faith we should be fearless; the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for Israel in chapter 7. To still fear the enemy shows a lack of faith, that you really do not believe in your God. Nehemiah shows the right spirit. In the Persian captivity he had liberty from the king to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and the enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem plotted to scare him off the work. A hired man urged him to hide in the temple because they were coming to slay him, and Nehemiah refused; operating in the spirit of fear is sin according to the scripture.

Samuel had instructed Saul in chapter 10: when you get to Gilgal, tarry seven days, make no moves until I arrive. Saul tarried seven days according to the set time, but Samuel came not at the moment expected, and the people were scattered from him and acting frantic. Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and he offered the burnt offering, and Saul is not the priest; that is Samuel's office. And it came to pass that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. He was barely late, and Saul could not hold his patience. Brothers do the same thing today: leadership said it would be here at ten, it is five past ten, so we cancel the plan and go home. Be humble and tarry like you were instructed; it may run some minutes over, and the Lord may be testing your patience.

Samuel asks, What hast thou done? Saul answers with excuses: the people were scattered from me, thou camest not within the days appointed, the Philistines gathered at Michmash, so I forced myself and offered a burnt offering. This is part of Saul's pattern of behavior; he never wants to hold himself accountable, he always deflects onto whoever else.

Samuel does not entertain the excuses: thou hast done foolishly; thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God. Saul thought he was only bending Samuel's word, but disobeying the instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. For now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever; but now thy kingdom shall not continue. For that one act of foolishness the Lord withdrew what he would have given: Saul's lineage ruling Israel. The Lord wants to see whether you will perform what he told you to do even when things do not work out how you planned; that is what proves you faithful in temptation and worthy of being exalted. Saul failed that test in the time of his distress. The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart to be captain over his people. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement; that man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures.

Samuel went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin, and Saul numbered the people present with him, about six hundred men. The Philistines encamped in Michmash, and the spoilers came out of their camp in three companies, toward Ophrah, toward Bethhoron, and toward the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim; three raiding parties sent out to invade Israel.

There was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears. The Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his share, his coulter, his axe, and his mattock, so the Philistines knew exactly how disarmed Israel was; all they had was a file for the tools. This is heavy for today. A people that must depend on its adversary for weaponry cannot deliver itself by arms; talk of going to war means nothing when you have to buy your weapons from the very gun store of the ones you say you will fight. Same picture as the scriptures. So in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear in the hand of any of the people, but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found; only two men in the army had a blade. In chapter 13 Saul blew the kingdom with his instability in a time of distress. The Most High said, You are not fit; I would have established you, but your replacement is already on the way.

Coming out of the prior chapters, Saul was hunting after David to kill him. When Saul returned from following the Philistines and was told David was in the wilderness of Engedi, he took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel to seek David and his men upon the rocks of the wild goats. Saul went into the cave to cover his feet: that means he was in there relieving himself. See the vulnerable position Saul was in, and yet David spared his life; that is why David could say, thou wast delivered into my hand, but I did not take thy life.

Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand: who is being referred to as the enemy? His own people; Saul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and David was of the tribe of Judah. On the skirt: the Zondervan Compact Bible Dictionary (page 136) shows the basic garments in general use among men of biblical times were the inner tunic, the tunic coat, the girdle, and the cloak, with the headdress and sandals. The word skirt in the KJV usually refers to an article of male, not female, clothing, with meanings of extremity and corner. Where we have our fringes attached to the borders of our garments, that is the bottom part of Saul's robe that David cut off privily.

When Saul rose out of the cave, David went out after him, cried, My lord the king, and stooped with his face to the earth and bowed himself. He reverenced Saul even though Saul was trying to kill him; that is why the Most High said David is a man after mine own heart. David maintained his integrity. David laid the proof before Saul: this day thine eyes have seen how the Lord delivered thee into mine hand in the cave, and some bade me kill thee, but mine eye spared thee, for he is the Lord's anointed. See the skirt of thy robe in my hand: I cut off the skirt and killed thee not; there is neither evil nor transgression in mine hand, yet thou huntest my soul to take it. David left the judgment with the Most High: the Lord judge between me and thee, and the Lord avenge me of thee, but mine hand shall not be upon thee; as saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked. After whom is the king of Israel come out? after a dead dog, after a flea.

Saul lifted up his voice and wept, and said to David, Thou art more righteous than I, for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil; if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? Saul made an acknowledgement there because he saw the righteousness of David: I know well that thou shalt surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in thine hand.

Saul asked David to swear that he would not cut off his seed after him nor destroy his name out of his father's house, and David sware unto Saul; Saul went home, and David and his men gat them up unto the hold. David showed so much restraint and respect unto his elder; that is something some of us struggle with today, and we need to use this as an example. The Most High was dealing with David: even though he saw Saul acting wickedly and strangely with him, when he had the opportunity to kill Saul he would not do it.

The Ziphites came unto Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon? Right here we are going back: chapter 26 is picking up on what we read in chapter 23, when the Ziphites first went up to Saul to deliver David into the king's hand.

David beheld the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his host; Saul lay in the trench with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster, and the people pitched round about him as protection to the king. David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai the son of Zeruiah, the brother of Joab, Who will go down with me to Saul to the camp? and Abishai said, I will go down with thee; and they came to the people by night, and all lay sleeping.

Abishai said, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day; let me smite him, I pray thee, with the spear even to the earth at once, and I will not smite him the second time. But David said, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed, and be guiltless? David left Saul's end with the Most High: as the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish; the Lord forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed. They took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster and got them away, and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the Lord was fallen upon them.

David went over to the other side, stood on the top of an hill afar off, and cried to Abner: Art not thou a valiant man? and who is like to thee in Israel? wherefore then hast thou not kept thy lord the king? for there came one of the people in to destroy the king thy lord. As the Lord liveth, ye are worthy to die, because ye have not kept your master, the Lord's anointed; and now see where the king's spear is, and the cruse of water that was at his bolster.

Saul knew David's voice and said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And David said, Wherefore doth my lord thus pursue after his servant? for what have I done? or what evil is in mine hand? Let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the Lord: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains.

Saul said, I have sinned: return, my son David, for I will no more do thee harm, because my soul was precious in thine eyes this day: behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly. Saul was acknowledging once more David's righteousness, because again David had an opportunity to kill Saul and did not put forth his hand. David answered, The Lord render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness: for the Lord delivered thee into my hand to day, but I would not stretch forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed. Again he showed compassion, restraint, and the fear of the Most High. That is what we have to get to as far as brotherly love: when we see each other, we see Christ in each other. That is what our nation is lacking, and that is why we have to be that example, as David was in sparing Saul's life.

When the king sat in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies round about, David said to Nathan the prophet that he dwelt in a house of cedar while the ark of God dwelt within curtains. David was not seeking his own riches but a place for the ark. Nathan told David to do all that was in his heart, for the Lord was with him. But that night the word of the Lord came to Nathan. The Lord asked, Shalt thou build me a house to dwell in? He had not dwelt in any house since bringing Israel out of Egypt but had walked in a tent and a tabernacle, and had never asked any tribe why they built Him not a house of cedar.

The Lord reminded David that He took him from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over His people Israel, and was with him whithersoever he went, cutting off all his enemies and making him a great name. The Most High promised to appoint a place for His people Israel and to plant them that they might dwell in a place of their own and move no more, and that the children of wickedness should afflict them no more. The Lord calls the nations the children of wickedness, the same as when it is taught that Esau is of the wicked one. He also promised David rest from all his enemies, and that the Lord Himself would make David a house.

The Lord said that when David's days were fulfilled and he slept with his fathers, He would set up his seed after him, proceeding out of his bowels, and establish his kingdom; that seed would build a house for the Lord's name. The word reaches past Solomon. Solomon built the house and sat on the throne, but his kingdom was not established for ever; his son Rehoboam would not hear counsel, and the kingdom split into two nations. The phrase "for ever" points to Jesus Christ the black Messiah, who came through David's lineage. The Lord said He would be his father and he His son, and if he committed iniquity He would chasten him with the rod of men. Solomon was not chastened with the rod of men in his lifetime; the one smitten with the rod upon the cheek was Jesus the Christ, who did no sin, though it was Solomon who sinned. The Lord promised that His mercy would not depart from him as it did from Saul, and that David's house, kingdom, and throne would be established for ever. The Lord did not make the Bible easy in every place, that He might see who would research and learn precept upon precept.

Nathan spoke to David according to all these words and this vision. Then David went in and sat before the Lord and said, Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto? David marveled that the Lord had spoken of his house for a great while to come, for there is none like the Most High, neither is there any God beside Him, according to all Israel had heard with their ears. David asked what one nation in the earth is like Israel, whom God went to redeem for a people to Himself, to make Him a name and to do great and terrible things. He did not redeem one man alone but a whole people, and He will bring them out again as a people. The teaching applies: though a brother or sister may have a difference, we must forgive one another and come back together, for the Most High chose us as one people. We lost our heritage in captivity, and coming back to it we must let go of grudges. The northern and southern kingdoms are to be made one nation again under one king and one shepherd. The one king is Jesus Christ, called the throne of David because David ruled over all twelve tribes; David will be present but is not the king. The chief shepherd, the great shepherd, the good shepherd who lays down his life is Christ, and he gathers the elect from the four winds and brings them up out of the land.

David prayed that the Lord would establish for ever the word He had spoken concerning His servant and his house, and do as He had said. He asked that the Lord's name be magnified for ever, that men would say, The Lord of hosts is the God of Israel, and that the house of His servant David be established before Him. Because the Lord of hosts had revealed to David that He would build him a house, David found in his heart to pray this prayer. He rested on the truth of the Lord's word, that with the Lord's blessing the house of His servant would be blessed for ever.

David smote the Philistines and subdued them, taking Methegammah out of their hand, and smote Moab, measuring them with a line, casting them to the ground. Our forefather David was a mighty warrior, subduing two different nations, which nations do not usually do at once. With two lines he measured Moab to death and with one full line to keep alive; the Moabites became David's servants and brought gifts. War was not about killing everyone, for the living become servants and pay tribute; the fear was put in the nations so they would not fight back. David smote Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates, taking a thousand chariots, seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen, houghing the chariot horses but reserving a hundred chariots. When the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer, David slew twenty and two thousand of them and put garrisons in Syria, and the Syrians became servants and brought gifts. The Lord preserved David whithersoever he went. David took the shields of gold and much brass and carried them to Jerusalem.

When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer, he sent his son Joram to salute and bless David, because Hadadezer had had wars with Toi. Joram brought vessels of silver, gold, and brass. This is the making of allies: when a stronger king removes an enemy you could never beat, the wise thing is to ally with him. David's kingdom made allies, but not by serving their idols or giving sons and daughters in marriage; the alliances served needful things, as Hiram later helped build the temple. David dedicated the silver and gold to the Lord, along with that dedicated from all the nations he subdued: Syria, Moab, the children of Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek, and the spoil of Hadadezer. David got a name when he returned from smiting the Syrians in the valley of salt, eighteen thousand men. He put garrisons throughout all Edom, and all they of Edom became David's servants, and the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went.

David reigned over all Israel and executed judgment and justice unto all his people. This is the mark of a real king and ruler: to lead the people in true judgment according to the commandments. The prayer of a servant is to one day have the spirit of King David, to lead brothers and sisters in justice and truth, and for all the brothers to become such leaders, each praying that those under them be better than themselves. David set his officers: Joab over the host; Jehoshaphat the recorder; Zadok and Ahimelech the priests; Seraiah the scribe; Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David's sons were chief rulers. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Abijam reigns three years in Jerusalem and walks in all the sins of his father, his heart not perfect with the Most High as David's was. The children did what they saw their fathers do, not merely what was said, which is why the Most High teaches His people to be different. Yet for David's sake the Most High gives him a lamp in Jerusalem, because David did right all his days save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, a wrong from which David repented. -

After Abijam dies, Asa his son reigns forty-one years and does right in the eyes of the Most High as David his father did. Asa takes the sodomites out of the land, removes the idols his fathers made, and even removes his own mother Maachah from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, which he destroys and burns at the brook Kidron. Though the high places are not removed, Asa's heart is perfect with the Most High all his days, and he brings dedicated silver, gold, and vessels into the house of the Most High.

There is war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel, who builds Ramah to cut off passage to and from Asa. Asa takes silver and gold from the house of the Most High and the king's house and sends it to Benhadad of Syria to break his league with Baasha, and Benhadad smites cities of Israel so Baasha stops building Ramah. Asa uses the stones and timber of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. In his old age he is diseased in his feet, then sleeps with his fathers, and Jehoshaphat his son reigns in his place.

Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel two years and does evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha conspires against him, kills him, and reigns in his place, then smites all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite. This fulfills, years later, the judgment that Jeroboam's descendants would be destroyed for the sins by which he made Israel to sin.

Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah and does evil, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin by which he made Israel to sin. The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming.

David loves the Most High, his strength, his rock, fortress, deliverer, buckler, the horn of his salvation and his high tower. He calls upon the Lord who is worthy to be praised, and so is saved from his enemies.

The sorrows of death compassed him and the floods of ungodly men made him afraid; the sorrows of hell compassed him and the snares of death prevented him. The sorrows of death describe the curses of the scattering. -

The earth shook and the foundations of the hills moved and were shaken because the Most High was wroth. Smoke went out of his nostrils and fire out of his mouth devoured. He bowed the heavens and came down with darkness under his feet; he rode upon a cherub and did fly upon the wings of the wind. He made darkness his secret place, dark waters and thick clouds his pavilion; at his brightness the clouds passed with hailstones and coals of fire. The Lord thundered in the heavens, the Most High gave his voice, and sent out his arrows and lightnings to scatter and discomfit his enemies. The channels of waters were seen and the foundations of the world were discovered at his rebuke, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.

He sent from above and drew David out of many waters, delivering him from his strong enemy and from them which hated him, for they were too strong for him. We are still looking for that deliverance from our strong enemy and them that hate us. -

The Lord rewarded David according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands, because he kept the ways of the Lord and did not wickedly depart from his God. We get clean by taking heed to the word and the commandments, not by water baptism. -

With the merciful the Most High shows himself merciful, with the upright man upright, with the pure pure, and with the froward he shows himself froward. He will save the afflicted people but bring down high looks. Israel is the afflicted people the scripture is talking about. -

The Most High lights David's candle and enlightens his darkness; by his God he has run through a troop and leaped over a wall. As for God, his way is perfect and the word of the Lord is tried; he is a buckler to all that trust in him. -

He teaches David's hands to war so that a bow of steel is broken by his arms; he gives him the shield of his salvation, his right hand holds him up, and his gentleness makes him great. He enlarges David's steps under him so his feet do not slip; David pursues his enemies, overtakes them, and does not turn again till they are consumed. -

His enemies cry but there is none to save them, even unto the Lord, but he answers them not; David beats them small as the dust before the wind and casts them out as dirt in the streets. The Most High delivers him from the strivings of the people and makes him the head of the heathen; a people whom he has not known shall serve him. -

The Lord liveth, blessed be his rock, and let the God of his salvation be exalted; it is God that avenges David and subdues the people under him. He delivers David from his enemies and lifts him above those that rise against him, delivering him from the violent man. The enemies are not just going to and fro; there is a people who serve satan, the so-called white man, to make it plain. -

Therefore David gives thanks among the heathen and sings praises to the Most High's name. Great deliverance he gives to his king and shows mercy to his anointed, to David and to his seed forevermore. -

Everyone that thirsts is called to the waters, and he that has no money is told to come, buy, and eat wine and milk without money and without price. The invitation is free. He asks why they spend money for that which is not bread and their labour for that which does not satisfy. They are told to hearken and eat that which is good, and let the soul delight itself in fatness. If they incline their ear and come, their soul will live, and He will make an everlasting covenant with them, even the sure mercies of David. David is given for a witness to the people, a leader and a commander. A nation not known will be called, and nations that did not know her will run to her because of the Most High, who has glorified her.

Seek the Most High while He may be found, call upon Him while He is near. The wicked is to forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and return to the Most High, who will have mercy and abundantly pardon. His thoughts are not our thoughts, and His ways are not our ways. As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are His ways and His thoughts higher than ours.

As the rain and snow come down from heaven and do not return without watering the earth, causing it to bring forth seed and bread, so His word does not return to Him void but accomplishes what He pleases. His people will go out with joy and be led forth with peace; the mountains and hills will break forth into singing and the trees of the field will clap their hands. Instead of the thorn will come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier the myrtle tree, and this will be to the Most High for a name and an everlasting sign that will not be cut off.

verses.text: But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the Lord commanded thee.

And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily.
And it came to pass afterward, that David’s heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
And he said unto his men, The Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the Lord’s anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the Lord.
So David stayed his servants with these words, and suffered them not to rise against Saul. But Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed, and be guiltless?
David said furthermore, As the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish.
The Lord forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the Lord’s anointed: but, I pray thee, take thou now the spear that is at his bolster, and the cruse of water, and let us go.
Now therefore so shalt thou say unto my servant David, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I took thee from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel:
And I was with thee whithersoever thou wentest, and have cut off all thine enemies out of thy sight, and have made thee a great name, like unto the name of the great men that are in the earth.

Moreover I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, that they may dwell in a place of their own, and move no more; neither shall the children of wickedness afflict them any more, as beforetime,
And as since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel, and have caused thee to rest from all thine enemies. Also the Lord telleth thee that he will make thee an house.

For he called upon the most high Lord; and he gave him strength in his right hand to slay that mighty warrior, and set up the horn of his people.
So the people honoured him with ten thousands, and praised him in the blessings of the Lord, in that he gave him a crown of glory.
For he destroyed the enemies on every side, and brought to nought the Philistines his adversaries, and brake their horn in sunder unto this day.
In all his works he praised the Holy One most high with words of glory; with his whole heart he sung songs, and loved him that made him.
He set singers also before the altar, that by their voices they might make sweet melody, and daily sing praises in their songs.
He beautified their feasts, and set in order the solemn times until the end, that they might praise his holy name, and that the temple might sound from morning.
The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.
